Niagara Falls. A cascade of three massive waterfalls on the Niagara River, which forms the border between New York and Ontario. Straddling the Canada-United States boundary, the falls represent one of North America's most recognizable natural wonders and a crucial source of hydroelectric power.

Niagara Falls drops approximately one hundred eighty-eight feet, or fifty-seven meters, from Lake Erie into the Niagara River, which flows into Lake Ontario.

The falls consist of three separate cascades: Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side, American Falls, and Bridal Veil Falls, with the Horseshoe Falls being the most powerful.

Over seven hundred fifty thousand gallons of water per second flow over the falls, making it one of the fastest-moving sections of the Niagara River.

The falls were formed about ten thousand years ago at the end of the last ice age when meltwater carved the Niagara Gorge.

First noted by European explorers in the sixteen hundreds, the falls quickly became famous as a natural wonder. Daredevils have attempted stunts over the falls since the eighteen hundreds.

Hydroelectric power stations harness the falls' energy. Today the falls supply electricity to millions in both Canada and the United States.

Niagara Falls remains a major tourist destination attracting millions annually, with illuminated nighttime displays adding to its spectacle.
